desc:
You are given a lowercase string s and a positive integer k. The vowels are a, e, i, o, u; every other letter is a consonant.

A non-empty substring is beautiful if, with v vowels and c consonants in it, both conditions hold:

  • v == c
  • (v * c) % k == 0

Return the number of beautiful substrings of s (substrings at different positions are counted separately).

s = "baeyh", k = 2
beautiful: "baey" (v=2, c=2) and "aeyh" (v=2, c=2); "ba" has v*c = 1, not divisible by 2
result = 2
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Checking all substrings is O(n2) and may pass small cases. Start with the condition v == c: map vowels to +1, consonants to -1 and use prefix sums.
Now the product condition: with v == c == len / 2 it becomes (len / 2)2 % k == 0, i.e. len2 % (4k) == 0. This holds for all multiples of one fixed number L.
Factorise 4k as a product of pe; then L is the product of pceil(e/2). Count pairs of prefixes with the same (balance, index % L) using a hash map.
editorial: Map each vowel to +1 and each consonant to -1; a substring has v == c iff its prefix balances at the two ends are equal. Then len = 2v, and the second condition v2 % k == 0 is the same as len2 % (4k) == 0.

For a prime power pe dividing 4k, len2 is divisible by it iff len is divisible by pceil(e/2). So len2 % 4k == 0 iff len % L == 0, where L is the product of those prime powers. Two prefix positions i < j then delimit a beautiful substring iff their balances are equal and j ≡ i (mod L) (so j - i is a multiple of L; the length is automatically even because the balance is zero).

Scan the string keeping a dictionary from (balance, index mod L) to the number of earlier prefixes with that key (the empty prefix is index 0 with balance 0). Each new prefix adds the stored count to the answer. Computing L takes O(sqrt(k)) and the scan is O(n) time and space; the brute-force alternative is O(n2).
